title: Boosting Multitask Learning on Graphs through Higher-Order Task Affinities

problem.claim: The paper studies simultaneous prediction of multiple node labeling functions on graphs from a multitask learning perspective.

gap.claim: Naive multitask learning can produce prevalent negative transfer because task relationships across node labeling functions are highly nonlinear.

contributions.claim: An algorithm clusters tasks into groups using a higher-order task affinity measure and fits a multitask model separately for each group as a boosting procedure over a baseline model.

The higher-order affinity between two tasks is estimated from one task's prediction loss in the presence of the other task and a random subset of additional tasks, followed by spectral clustering for task grouping.
The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that, under a planted block model of tasks on graphs, the affinity scores can provably separate tasks into groups.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their speedup techniques compute higher-order affinity scores efficiently and that the scores predict negative transfers more accurately than pairwise task affinities.
The authors report favorable results against existing methods on various community detection and molecular graph prediction data sets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Node-label prediction on graphs is established and broadly applicable.
The paper formulates simultaneous prediction of multiple node labeling functions as graph multitask learning, with overlapping community detection as an example.
Naive multitask learning suffers prevalent negative transfer because task relationships are highly nonlinear.
The proposed procedure estimates higher-order task affinities, clusters tasks spectrally, and fits multitask models by group with computational speedups.
The authors report favorable empirical results and a theoretical task-separation guarantee under a planted block model.

source_observation.claim: Task relationships may be nonlinear and may cause negative transfer when multiple graph-labeling tasks are trained together.

interpretation.claim: Multitask systems may benefit from identifying compatible task groups instead of sharing information across all tasks.

application.claim: For graph multitask learning, evaluate task grouping and higher-order affinities before applying a single shared multitask model.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that the procedure generalizes beyond the reported data sets or task model assumptions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the data sets, dataset sizes, baselines, or quantitative performance values.
The abstract does not provide the formal planted block model assumptions or the proof details.
The abstract does not quantify the computational speedups or define the baseline multitask model.
